title: 8,000 steps on one or two days a week: what ten years of death records show [threshold, ard_1_2]
teaser: Among 3,101 US adults, reaching 8,000 steps on only 1 to 2 days a week was associated with a 10-year risk of death 14.9 points lower than never reaching it. [sample, threshold, ard_1_2, followup] The comparison is less clean than it sounds. [-]
hook: Step counts are usually sold as a daily target. [-] This study asked a different question: does it matter on how many days of the week you get there? [threshold]
populationPanel: Who was studied: 3,101 US adults aged 20 or older who wore a step counter for 1 week in 2005-2006. [sample, cohort] National death records then followed them. [cohort] Nobody was assigned to walk more or less, so this is an observational study. [cohort] It describes these adults. It is not a prescription. [-]

card.question: Do one or two 8,000-step days a week go with a longer life? [threshold]
card.headline: People with 1–2 such days had a 14.9-point lower 10-year risk of death than people with none. [ard_1_2, followup, threshold]
card.support: This is the difference after the study's adjustments. [ard_1_2]

glance.x: Days a week at the step goal [-]
glance.alt: Two grids of dots, one for people who never reached the step goal and one for people who did on one or two days a week. [threshold] Hollow dots are people who died within ten years, before any adjustment. [crude_0, crude_1_2]
glance.note: Each dot is a person, before any adjustment. Try it with your own week inside. [-]

paragraphs: Picture a ramp that falls steeply, then levels off. [-] The biggest gap in risk sits between people with no 8,000-step days and people with one or two. [ard_1_2, ard_3_7, threshold] Past three or four such days a week, the curve was nearly flat. [plateau]

The same shape shows up for steps per day. [parallel_meta] In an earlier pooled analysis, risk stopped falling at 6,000 to 8,000 steps a day for adults over 60. [parallel_meta] For younger adults it stopped at 8,000 to 10,000. [parallel_meta]
Studies of exercise point the same way. [nhis_prior] In a large US survey, death risks showed no clear difference between weekend-only exercisers and people active all week. [nhis_prior]
So 8,000 is a handy marker, not a magic line. [thresholds, threshold] Any daily cut-off from 6,000 to 10,000 steps gave similar results. [thresholds]

The study counted days, not daily totals. [threshold] People wore a step counter for one week. [cohort] Researchers then sorted them by how many days they reached 8,000 steps: none, 1 to 2, or 3 to 7. [threshold] National death records followed them for about 10 years. [cohort, followup]

The researchers allowed for age, health and habits. [models] After that, people with 1 to 2 such days had a 10-year risk of death 14.9 points lower than people with none. [ard_1_2, followup] With 3 to 7 days it was 16.5 points, only a little more. [ard_3_7]

audit.effect: Adjusted risk difference, 1 to 2 days against none: a 10-year risk of death 14.9 points lower. [ard_1_2, followup]
audit.weakEnd: The 95% confidence interval runs from 18.8 points to 10.9 points lower. [ard_1_2] Even the weak end, 10.9 points, is a wide gap for a study of deaths. [ard_1_2] The range cannot say whether the walking is the reason. [ard_1_2]
limitations: The study counted steps for one week only, at the start. [one_week] How these people walked over the next 10 years is unknown. [one_week, followup]
This is an observational study. [cohort] Poor health can mean fewer steps and an earlier death, and no adjustment removes that fully. [confounding]
Wearing a tracker can make people more active that week, putting some usually inactive people in the wrong group. [hawthorne, reactivity_misclassification]
audit.missed: The adjusted gap was 7.4 points in adults under 65 and 19.9 points in those 65 and over. [ard_1_2_under65, ard_1_2_65plus] The adjustments shrank it: 18.7 points with age and sex alone, 14.9 with everything. [ard_1_2_agesex, ard_1_2]
more: Heart and blood vessel deaths showed the same pattern: 8.1 points lower for 1 to 2 days, 8.4 for 3 to 7. [cv_ard_1_2, cv_ard_3_7, threshold]
The study kept only people who wore the tracker for the week, which may bias the sample. [selection_bias]

figure.title: Why the raw gap is so wide [-]
figure.headline: The three groups were different people before anyone counted a step. [ages, mobility]
figure.caption: Poor health can affect both step counts and survival. [confounding] The study adjusted for much of this, not all. [models, confounding] Steps were counted for one week only. [one_week]
figure.alt: Three columns, one for each group: no days, 1 to 2 days and 3 to 7 days a week at 8,000 steps or more. [threshold] The average ages are 63.7, 51.5 and 46.0 years. [ages] The shares with trouble walking or climbing stairs are 50.5%, 20.3% and 6.8%. [mobility, mobility_def]

params.mobilityWords: had trouble walking or with stairs

glossary.plain: A small device worn on the body that records movement; here it counted steps for a week.
Allowances the researchers made for how the groups differed, such as age, smoking and illness, so that like is compared with like.

takeaways: If a daily target keeps failing, the study's lowest active group is a reasonable place to start: 8,000 steps on 1 to 2 days a week. [threshold, ard_1_2]
Past 3 to 4 such days the association flattened, so a missed day is no reason to write off the week. [plateau]
The association was widest in adults aged 65 and over, at 19.9 points against 7.4 points in younger adults. [ard_1_2_65plus, ard_1_2_under65]

The headline number [-]
slides.body: After adjustment, people with 1 to 2 such days had a 10-year risk of death 14.9 points lower than people with none. [ard_1_2, followup]

slides.heading: More days added little [-]
slides.body: At 3 to 7 days the gap was 16.5 points. [ard_3_7] The curve went flat at 3 to 4 days. [plateau]

slides.heading: Who this describes [-]
slides.body: 3,101 US adults aged 20 or older, tracked for 1 week, then traced through death records. [sample, cohort] Observational: nobody was assigned to walk. [cohort]

slides.heading: The groups were not alike [-]
slides.body: Mean age was 63.7 in the zero-day group and 46.0 in the 3-to-7-day group. [ages, threshold] Adjustment narrows that difference. It cannot erase it. [confounding]

slides.heading: What this cannot show [-]
slides.body: Steps were measured for 1 week only. [one_week] People in poor health walk less, so part of the gap is illness, not walking. [confounding]
